thesis: Joseph-Marie Jacquard built a loom that wove complex patterns automatically by reading a chain of punched cards, each hole lifting one thread. Holes and no-holes are binary, and his cards led through Babbage and IBM to the stored numbers inside AI models.

story.title: Cards that weave
story.text: Jacquard demonstrated a loom attachment that read a chain of punched cards. Where a card had a hole, a hook passed through and lifted its warp thread; where it had none, the thread stayed down. The shuttle carried the weft under the lifted threads, and the next card set up the next row.

story.title: Change the cards, change the cloth
story.text: Weaving a pattern means lifting a different set of warp threads for every pass of the shuttle. Before Jacquard, a helper lifted them by hand. Each card holds one row of the pattern, and the chain repeats. Swapping or re-punching the cards makes the same loom weave a completely different design.

story.title: Holes, bits, pixels
story.text: Holes and no-holes are binary. Babbage planned to program his Analytical Engine with Jacquard cards, and Herman Hollerith's punched cards processed the 1890 US census, a business that grew into IBM. A woven picture is a grid of 1s and 0s, like the pixels an image AI reads, and a trained model is a vast stored pattern.

hint: Click holes on the current card to punch or fill them, and watch that row of the cloth and its 1s and 0s change on the next repeat.
